subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Aqueous Cu²⁺ ions are blue in colour whereas aqueous Zn²⁺ ions are colourless. Why?

mark_split.label: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ and has an unpaired d electron

verification.note: Unit 11 (d and f Block Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 8 ("8. d & f BLOCK ELEMENTS"), book pp.91-94, which prints this question on book p.91 as VSAQ 5. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK NOTATION: the printed question writes Cu+2 and Zn+2; Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are used here. BOOK GAP FILLED: the printed answer stops at the electron count and does not say WHY an unpaired d electron produces colour, so the card adds the two missing links — the water ligands split the d orbitals, and the d-d transition removes one colour from white light, leaving its complement. TREND AND EXCEPTION NAMED HERE: most first-series ions in water are coloured and paramagnetic, and the exceptions are the two ends — Sc³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ at 3d⁰, and Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺ at 3d¹⁰ — all four colourless and diamagnetic. MAGNETIC MOMENTS COMPUTED: Cu²⁺ has n = 1, so μ = √3 = 1.73 BM; Zn²⁺ has n = 0, so μ = 0 BM.

steps.label: Cu²⁺ is blue
lines: Cu²⁺ loses the 4s electron and one 3d
It has one unpaired d electron, so n = 1
Water molecules around the ion split the
d orbitals into t2g and eg sets.
The eg set is left with one vacancy, so
a t2g electron is promoted into it.

steps.why: A d-d transition needs a partly filled d subshell, because the electron must have somewhere to move to. Cu²⁺ at 3d⁹ has exactly one vacancy, and the gap produced by the six water ligands corresponds to orange-red light, so what passes through is the complementary blue. The unpaired electron also makes the ion paramagnetic, with a spin-only moment of 1.73 BM.
common_mistakes: Writing Cu²⁺ as 3d⁷ 4s². Copper metal is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, so Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ 4s⁰.
Saying the blue is the colour of water. Pure water is colourless; the colour comes from the d-d transition in the hydrated ion.
steps.memory_tip: One vacancy in the d set is enough for colour. 3d⁹ has one; 3d¹⁰ has none.
steps.margin_note: Give the configuration, then the words unpaired d electron, then d-d transition. All three together earn this mark.

Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) is colourless for the opposite
reason: its d subshell is empty.
steps.why: The colourless ions of the first series are the ones with no partly filled d subshell. Sc³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ are 3d⁰ and have no electron to promote; Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺ are 3d¹⁰ and have no vacancy to promote into. Every ion with a partly filled d subshell, 3d¹ to 3d⁹, is both coloured and paramagnetic. Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺, the two named on this card, are also diamagnetic, which is the same fact stated for magnetism instead of colour.
common_mistakes: Saying Zn²⁺ has no d electrons. It has ten; the point is that no empty d orbital is left in the same set.
Saying all d-block ions are coloured. Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺ are all colourless.
steps.memory_tip: Empty d⁰ or full d¹⁰ means colourless. Anything in between is coloured.
steps.margin_note: Name Sc³⁺ beside Zn²⁺. It shows the rule works from both ends of the series.

insider_note: Marks here are given for a d-electron count on both ions, not only on the coloured one. Adding Sc³⁺ as the empty-d case takes one line and is usually read as full understanding.
